prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 92px · one-line width 452px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 67px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 69px · one-line width 69px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 64px · one-line width 68px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 70px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 557px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 556px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"All headers and numbers stay on one line and nothing breaks, but the label column is starved (~170px) so the metric names wrap to 4–5 lines (e.g. 'Net revenue / retention, / trailing twelve / months'), inflating row heights and stretching the vertical distance between a row's numbers, while the numeric columns sit wide with unused slack."},"B":{"grade":"bad","why":"The label column is squeezed so hard that 'percentage' splits mid-word ('percentag / e of'), and labels run to 5–6 short lines ('Net revenue / retention, / trailing / twelve / months'), giving ragged, broken text next to over-wide numeric columns that need none of that space."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Well-proportioned: all five headers sit on one line, every number and identifier stays intact, and the ~210px label column wraps long metrics into 2–4 tidy lines without orphans or word breaks; rows read as compact units and the four year columns form an even rhythm for left-to-right comparison."},"D":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Essentially the same balanced solution as C with the label column a touch narrower and the year columns a touch wider; headers and figures all fit on one line, labels break at sensible points ('Customer acquisition / cost, blended'), and no column looks padded or pinched."},"E":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Labels wrap nicely and numbers are intact, but the FY 2024 column is narrower than its peers, so its header breaks into 'FY / 2024' while the other year headers stay single-line — the header band becomes uneven and one year column reads as second-class."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"Best label wrapping of the narrow-header group (long metrics fall into two clean lines such as 'Sales and marketing expense as a / percentage of revenue'), but it repeats the flaw of a pinched FY 2024 column whose header wraps to 'FY / 2024', breaking the symmetry of the four comparable year headers."}},"best":["C","D"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"Exact pixel widths are estimated from the renders; whether B's mid-word split ('percentag/e') is a genuine width effect or an artefact of the review harness, and whether C/D's numeric columns are marginally tighter than the 68–70px content needs."}
